blocks.en: Welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today we start with big football news: a true king of football has played his last game for his country.
Then we dive under the sea to meet a tiny shrimp with amazing eyes.
Let's jump in!
Lionel Messi has played his last game for Argentina.
In his farewell match against Benin, the blue and white team won three-zero, and Messi was the star of the night: he scored one goal and made two assists — he had a hand in every goal of the game.
More than eighty-five thousand fans filled the Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires to say goodbye.
Messi first played for Argentina twenty-one years ago.
He has played two hundred and eight games for his country and scored one hundred and twenty-six goals — more than any other Argentine player in history.
With Argentina, Messi won the World Cup and two Copa América titles.
After the game, he told his fans: "Yesterday was my last game, and I already miss wearing the blue and white."
For Messi, that famous shirt is like a second skin — saying goodbye was not easy.
And here is the warmest part of the story.
Cristiano Ronaldo, Messi's greatest rival for twenty years, left a message under Messi's post: "Leo, so many years defending your country, and a story that will live on forever.
You have all my respect.
A hug."
Two kings, one kind message: great rivals can also be great friends.
Their story will inspire young players for years to come.
Now meet the mantis shrimp, a small sea animal with a very big superpower.
It is famous for two things: a punch faster than a speeding bullet, and truly amazing eyes.
Your eyes have three kinds of color sensors.
The mantis shrimp has many, many more.
Scientists from Belgium and Germany studied seventeen light pigments inside its eyes.
Pigments are the tiny parts that catch light and turn it into pictures for the brain.
They found something nobody expected: four of the pigments work like tiny light switches.
Red light can switch them on, and blue light can switch them back off.
Other pigments answer to blue and orange light.
With all these clever switches, the shrimp can see colors of light that our eyes cannot see at all.
Why does this matter to us?
Doctors dream of tools that use light to switch tiny parts of the body on and off — a little like fixing a machine with a flashlight.
The shrimp's eyes may give scientists new ideas for such tools.
Nature, once again, built it first!
Here's today's idiom: "hang up your boots."
Football players wear special boots to play.
When a player retires and stops playing, we say he hangs up his boots — he puts them away and does not wear them again.
For example: "Messi has hung up his boots for Argentina, but he still plays for his club team."
Hanging up your boots for one team does not always mean goodbye to football forever!
So — one day, when your grandpa says he is too old to play football with you on Sundays, you can smile and say: "Grandpa has hung up his boots!"
But be careful — he might just put them back on!
That brings us to the end of today's show!
Here's a question: If your favorite player played one last game, what would you say to him?
"Thank you"?
"Please don't go"?
Or "Can I have your boots"?
Have a wonderful day, and see you tomorrow morning!
